findings.claim: Forcing `abortEarly: true` can make `validate()` diverge from `parse()`/`safeParse()` for schemas that internally tolerate or aggregate issues (unions, `.catch()`, pipes, coercion fallbacks).
findings.rationale: `validate()` is supposed to answer the same question as `safeParse(...).success`. Abort-early semantics propagate into nested runs; for constructs like `$ZodUnion` (which deliberately runs every option and inspects each option's issues) or `$ZodCatch` (which swallows inner issues), an early abort at the first issue can surface a failure to the outer payload before the recovering logic gets a chance to run, producing a false `false`. I have not traced every schema implementation, so confidence is moderate — but this is the kind of change that needs a test over union/catch/default/pipe schemas to confirm result parity with `safeParse`.

findings.claim: `abortEarly` may not be a member of `ParseContextInternal` / may not be honored at runtime, making this either a TS excess-property error or a silent no-op.
findings.rationale: In zod v4 core, the public `ParseContext` exposes `error`, `reportInput`, `jitless`, and the internal one adds `async`; abort semantics are normally driven per-payload (`continue`/`aborted` flags) rather than by a context flag. The second branch is an object literal assigned to an annotated type, so an unknown property would be an excess-property error; if the property does type-check but nothing reads `ctx.abortEarly`, the change does nothing at all. Worth verifying the flag is actually plumbed through `_zod.run`.

findings.claim: Caller-supplied `abortEarly: false` (and the expectation that all user refinements run) is silently overridden.
findings.rationale: The spread of `_ctx` is immediately overwritten, so a caller who configured full issue collection gets abort-early behavior instead. More importantly for side effects: user `.refine`/`.superRefine`/`.check` callbacks that previously all executed on the fallback path will now stop at the first issue, while the compiled fast path (when taken) may still run them all — so the observable number of user-callback invocations becomes dependent on whether JIT compilation kicked in. That also interacts with the adjacent comment about keeping user callbacks to an 'at-most-twice bound'.
